title: Set up your toolkit
why: The tools every developer uses every day. Once these are set up, everything else plugs into them.
learn: saving every version of your code, online
the code editor, plus its extensions
running JavaScript outside the browser and installing libraries
build: June v0.0
Put a “Hello, I'm June” page online with GitHub Pages.

title: Modern JavaScript and your first June
why: You already know JavaScript. Now learn the parts used to talk to servers and build real apps, and connect June to a brain for the first time.
learn: how your page asks a server for something and waits for the answer
the text format apps and AIs use to exchange data
JavaScript with safety checks that catch mistakes early
the standard way to build web apps today
keeping secret API keys out of your code
API, tokens, context window, temperature, streaming, system prompt
build a model adapter with simulated responses before connecting a local model or optional paid API
build: June v0.1
A text chat app with a model adapter and a June system prompt. Begin with simulated replies; connect a small local model or an optional paid API, and stream real responses.

title: June gets a face
why: The glowing network brain from the videos. This is pure front-end work, so it's the most fun place to use the skills you already have.
learn: drawing and animating hundreds of connected dots and lines with JavaScript
3D in the browser: particles, lines, glow, orbit rings and camera
measuring how loud a sound is, many times a second, so the orb can react to it
tiny programs that run on the graphics chip for glowing, flowing effects
designing how the orb looks when idle, listening, thinking and speaking
build: June v0.2
June's living brain: coloured clusters of connected dots around a glowing core, with signals firing between them. It reacts to music or your microphone and has four moods.

title: June gets a voice
why: Use free local Whisper for English voice input and an available local female English voice for replies. Prefer Indian English when available, label the actual accent, and review the transcript before sending.
learn: recognition versus synthesis; June uses local system synthesis because browser recognition services can fail
capture a short microphone recording, transcribe it locally with Whisper base.en after release, then review and edit the words
read replies with a selected local female system voice; hosted voices are optional later alternatives
queue complete sentences while model text arrives, flush on completion and cancel stale speech
Wiring the orb to her voice
measure recording audio; use speech lifecycle events and label synthesis movement as a visual approximation
wait for available voices, prefer female Indian English when present, label the actual accent and save your choice
build: June v0.3.1
Record a request, transcribe it on your Mac, review the words, send them to local June and hear her reply in the selected female voice. Stop releases recording, transcription and speech.

title: Python, the language of AI
why: The real-time voice tools, AI libraries and training tools you'll use from Phase 5 onwards are mostly written in Python.
learn: installing libraries without breaking other projects
running code in small pieces and seeing results straight away
doing several things at once, which live voice needs
a Python server that streams audio and text back and forth with your app
build: June v0.3.5
Move June's brain and voice calls into a Python backend that your web app talks to.
res: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python
Automate the Boring Stuff with Python

title: Real-time conversation
why: The step that makes people say “wait, that's real?”. No buttons: you speak from across the room, she answers with a measured response delay, and you can cut her off mid-sentence.
learn: Pipecat or LiveKit Agents, which connect ears, brain and voice with very little delay
“Hey June” detected on your own computer with Porcupine or openWakeWord
knowing when you've started and stopped talking (Silero VAD)
June stops talking the moment you interrupt her
not cutting you off when you pause to think
the technology video calls use to send live audio quickly
separate pieces vs one speech-to-speech model (see below)
build: June v0.4
Say “Hey June”, have a conversation and interrupt her. Measure response time and work toward a one-second first-audio target with suitable hardware.

title: Memory and personality
why: Give June a consistent style and user-controlled application memory. Use the workshop as a starting point; this does not train the model.
learn: writing instructions that get reliable, in-character answers
turning your workshop answers into June's system prompt
short spoken sentences, natural fillers like “hmm”, no lists or emoji
private SQLite chats on this Mac for 30 days; hosted Postgres/Supabase is optional later
June suggests facts with exact supporting quotes; only approved facts inform later chats
adjusting her voice's speed, warmth and emphasis to match her mood
ask before saving a fact; let the user review, correct, export and delete it
build: June v0.5

Review and approve suggested facts, recall them after New chat and restart, and manage a ten-field personality. Chats expire after 30 days; approved memories persist. Voice expression is a preference, not a guarantee of model consistency.

title: RAG: giving June knowledge
why: RAG means “look it up, then answer”. June searches your notes and documents first, then answers from what she found. You add knowledge without retraining anything.
learn: turning text into lists of numbers that capture its meaning
storing embeddings and finding the closest matches (pgvector on Supabase, or Chroma)
splitting long documents into small pieces
finding candidate pieces, then keeping only the best ones
June says where she found the answer
build: June v0.6
Ask June out loud about your own notes or PDFs and she answers from them, telling you where the answer came from.

title: June's hands: agents, MCP and your world
why: Connect tools one capability at a time: your Mac, home, email, job applications, editable websites/designs, PDF/PPTX files and transaction preparation. Permissions, review, cancellation and result verification belong in each project before live actions. A desktop wrapper is optional for tools available through the local server.
learn: Electron or Tauri, which wrap your web app into a real Mac app with a menu-bar icon and a global shortcut
June plans, uses a tool, checks the result, and repeats until the job is done
a standard plug that connects June to apps like Calendar, GitHub, Spotify and Notion
opening apps and running Apple Shortcuts when you ask
lights, fans and plugs through Home Assistant, which has its own MCP server
sending a screenshot to the brain so June can see what you're looking at
a spoken morning briefing, reminders and check-ins at times you set
authorise each account separately, restrict scopes and support revoking access
prepare an exact transaction for review; confirm changed prices and prevent duplicate purchases
allowlist Mac actions and home devices; check the result before saying done
build: June v0.7
Say “June, open VS Code and play my focus playlist” and it happens. Every morning she greets you with your weather, calendar and goals.
res: MCP servers you can plug in

title: How AI brains actually work
why: Optional model-learning track. Understand model internals and build a deliberately tiny model as an exercise. You can continue from Phase 8 to Phase 11 and deployment without this track; training from scratch is not required for fine-tuning or a useful assistant.
learn: vectors, matrices, probability and gradients, all taught with pictures
how a model learns by adjusting millions of numbers
the main library for building and training models
the design behind Claude, GPT and every modern language model
how text is chopped into pieces and turned into numbers
build: June-nano
Train a tiny GPT on text you may use, to understand next-token learning. This is a learning model, not a capable personal assistant.
res: Andrej Karpathy: Neural Networks, Zero to Hero

title: June's own brain and voice
why: Optional adaptation track. Start only when a measured behaviour gap remains after model selection, prompts, RAG and tools. Compare an adapter with the baseline and choose a voice separately. A GPU may support larger models and experiments; it does not guarantee frontier-model reliability.
learn: your workshop answers grown into a full document of values, tone and rules
reviewed June conversations, cleaned and deduplicated, with separate validation and test sets; see the training guide
training a small add-on to a free model (Qwen or Llama) with Unsloth or Hugging Face TRL
teaching June to prefer replies that sound like her
an original voice designed in ElevenLabs, or an open voice model like Kokoro or Piper that you run yourself
evaluate a small local brain, speech recognition and a licensed female voice on suitable hardware; offline performance must be measured
quantize the base model, train adapters, and hold out entire conversations for evaluation
prepare data on your Mac and use a GPU notebook first; see the hardware guide
build: June v1.0
June uses an evaluated adapter and a separately chosen voice. Test offline conversation on suitable hardware; online services still need internet.
res: Unsloth docs and free Colab notebooks

title: Testing and safety
why: An assistant that can control your computer and hears everything has to be trustworthy. Consolidate checks already introduced alongside every feature. Do not wait until this phase to protect accounts, files or transactions.
learn: a fixed set of test questions you run after every change, so you notice if June gets worse
checking that June sounds like June, using a strong model as the judge
June asks before sending messages, spending money or deleting anything
ignoring instructions hidden in web pages, emails or screenshots she reads
the wake word runs on your device, a visible “listening” light, and recordings you can delete
logging every conversation, delay and cost with Langfuse
test disconnected devices, revoked accounts, duplicate requests and price changes before enabling real actions
build: June v1.1
A 100-question test suite covering personality, accuracy, speed and safety, with a page showing her scores over time.

title: Going live and onto devices
why: June leaves your desk: a polished Mac app, a phone app, and a small speaker that sits in your room.
learn: installers, auto-updates and starting June when your Mac starts
React Native with Expo, using the JavaScript you already know
a Raspberry Pi with a microphone and speaker running the wake word and voice
Supabase Auth, Vercel for the website, a suitable model host using serving software such as vLLM
voice services charge by the minute, so cache what you can and use cheaper models for easy questions
packaging and automatic deployment with GitHub Actions
keep the home controller and voice endpoint separate from occasional model-training compute
build: June v2
Talk to June from your Mac, your phone, or a speaker in your room. She's the same June, with the same memory, everywhere.
